extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / early-18th-century polite society (educated men and women)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive social, linguistic and moral guidance aimed at members of polite society (particularly women and household heads), covering language usage, devotional reading, sexual/marriage conduct, party behaviour, and household stewardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of who/which (petition for grammatical justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners complain that 'THAT' and 'WHICH' have been preferred to 'WHO' in many places (Pulpits, the Bar, Acts of Parliament, prayers), degrading the proper distinctions of speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petition demands that 'Who' be used for persons and 'Which' for things (example complaint: 'Our Father WHICH art in Heaven' should be 'Our Father WHO art in Heaven'). The surrounding argument appeals to justice and propriety in language; no formal prescriptive rules are supplied beyond the demand that each retain its proper place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical acceptability of 'that' and expletives in discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejoinder defends the common use of 'that' and related expletive phrases, arguing they are useful and often necessary for natural discourse ('Such Things as That', 'That is', 'That is to say').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defence: resist rigid reform to eliminate 'that'—it facilitates length and flow in speech; examples cited include oratorical and colloquial uses, and the claim that some expressions ('Egad and all That') are rhetorically effective. Anti-pattern: forcing replacements that make speech clumsy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose devotional books that elevate the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting books of devotion for women (or private readers), preference should be given to those which 'elevate the Mind above the World, and give a pleasing Indifference to little things in it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'weekly preparations' and 'limited Godliness' which foster mechanical religion; prefer works that make virtue inward and cultivate genuine moral feeling. Example anti-pattern: devotional compilations that only produce a show of piety and permit worldly indulgence the rest of the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical or performative religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Devotional practice should not be a mechanical routine or outward show that leaves the mind untouched by true virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticised behaviour: reading many prayers mechanically or using devotional hours as a curtain for worldly pleasures (e.g., spending 6–8 hours at cards but still keeping one hour of prayer). Desired behaviour: inward transformation and moral improvement; the reader who is truly virtuous will have pity for vice, not only the absence of visible faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female virtues should be domestic and modest
rubrics_metrics.description: Women are urged to 'aspire only to those virtues that are peculiar to your Sex; follow your natural Modesty, and think it your greatest Commendation not to be talked of one way or other.' Female virtues are described as of a 'Domestick Turn.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended roles: tender mothers, faithful wives, guardians of the household. Anti-pattern: public, furious partisanship and competing for public distinction (e.g., using fashion or patches to signal party). Historical appeal: Pericles' funeral oration as authority for modesty and domestic focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not convert fashion into political signalling
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of women using cosmetic 'patches' to declare Whig or Tory allegiance; this practice aggravates public hatreds and diminishes the peculiar charms of women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: avoid partisan displays in dress or cosmetics; if showing public spirit, prefer acts that unite or serve the common good (example: ladies sacrificing rings/jewels for public exigence) rather than signalling factional disputes. Anti-pattern: deliberately patching one side of the face to mark party affiliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtship and marriage: value inward virtue over appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning against 'loving by Sight' which leads to accepting unworthy partners (coxcombs) and to changing affections frequently; advocates loving 'laudable Things' not mere external attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to young women: do not be guided solely by appearance; cultivate appreciation for moral qualities and accomplishments. Anti-pattern: delaying or choosing marriage primarily for distinction, amusement, or transient admiration; parents' unwise expenditure to fuel rivalry is also criticised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hypocrisy: outward piety must be matched by inward goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people call themselves virtuous by merely being free from obvious vice; this is condemned when outward devotional acts mask inward vice (e.g., insolent behaviour by one who appears pious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True virtue should be accompanied by pity of vice and inward moral sensibility. Examples: 'Dulcianara' is outwardly irreproachable in appearance yet insolent to friends; such inconsistency is an anti-pattern to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household financial prudence and simple accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation for modest, orderly management of household affairs: keep business within a narrow compass, require proper vouchers from a steward, and keep inventories (shirts, cravats, handkerchiefs, stockings) with numbers for reckoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical practices: have a steward supply receipts ready for signing; maintain an 'implement' (list) with items and counts to track laundress and expenditures. Anti-pattern: extravagance upon sudden fortune leading to ruin; same small-mindedness shows in both insolence in riches and shamelessness in poverty.

rubrics_metrics.name: When practising public zeal, direct it at genuine common enemies
rubrics_metrics.description: If women must show zeal for public matters, they should focus on opponents of 'their Faith, Liberty and Country' rather than quarrels among family or co-religionists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended public spirit: acts that defend the common good and unite rather than inflame domestic divisions. Example: Roman ladies contributing jewels in time of foreign danger as a laudable public act that warranted civic recognition.
